analysis.one_liner: Requires millionaires to pay at least 30% of their income in taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added a new "fair share tax" requiring any household with adjusted gross income above $1 million to pay at least 30% of income above that level in combined federal income and payroll taxes, after subtracting charitable donations. Its aim was to stop situations where millionaires pay lower effective tax rates than middle-class workers, and to use the revenue to cut the deficit. It also stated the Senate's view that Congress should pass broader tax reform closing loopholes used by the wealthy. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote; it died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would no longer watch millionaires pay lower effective rates than they do, and future taxpayers generally, since the revenue raised would go to deficit reduction rather than new spending. Middle-income households would pay nothing new; the tax only applies above $1 million of income.

how_it_helps.text: It imposes a minimum 30% tax rate on the portion of income above $1 million for households earning more than that, so the wealthiest can no longer pay a lower effective rate than middle-class families.
The revenue is framed as deficit reduction — cutting the deficit 'by billions of dollars a year' — rather than new spending, easing debt burdens that fall on future taxpayers.
Charitable contributions are carved out of the 30% base, so the bill does not penalize giving by wealthy donors.

analysis.who_pays: Households with adjusted gross income above $1 million, who would owe up to 30% of income above that threshold in combined income and payroll taxes after charitable deductions. No one else bears a direct cost.

drawbacks.text: The tax is targeted narrowly: it applies only to income above $1 million (with a phase-in above that threshold) and leaves the underlying deductions and loopholes that let high earners pay low rates fully intact, so it raises relatively little compared with broader tax reform.

High-income taxpayers could still reduce the tax through charitable deductions, which the bill explicitly carves out of the 30% base, so the effective rate on some very large incomes could still fall below 30%.

It is a minimum-rate patch on top of the existing tax code rather than the fundamental simplification its own 'sense of the Senate' section calls for, adding one more parallel tax computation alongside the existing alternative minimum tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — billions a year in deficit reduction paid by households already above $1 million, with a carve-out so charitable giving is not discouraged — is real and the cost to anyone else is essentially zero. The bill is narrower than its rhetoric suggests: it leaves most loopholes untouched and would raise only a modest share of what broader tax reform could. But as a floor on taxes for the highest earners, the design is sound; the failure is that it never received any committee or floor action in the Finance Committee over two years.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on February 13, 2013, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance — the only action it ever received.
The Finance Committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor.
It died at the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015, without ever coming to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy taxpayers whose effective tax rates stay below 30%, and anyone who benefits from the deficits those lower rates contribute to, are better off because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 13 cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents.

for.name: 13 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Baldwin, Blumenthal, Leahy, Reed, Lautenberg, Levin, Sanders, Rockefeller, Harkin, and Franken.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote — keeping it off the Senate floor for the entire Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed raising taxes on high earners as a matter of party position, and with enough seats to block tax legislation in the Senate, made consideration of such bills a non-starter.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Sen. Sanders; no Republican supported it, and the bill never advanced in the Democratic-controlled Finance Committee either.

industries.note: The bill would guarantee that millionaires pay at least 30% of income above the first million in combined income and payroll taxes, closing the gap that lets some of the richest taxpayers pay lower effective rates than ordinary wage earners.

A minimum rate would shrink the payoff from strategies that convert salary into lower-taxed income, reducing demand for sophisticated avoidance work, though the effect is modest since the underlying loopholes remain.
